added_lemmas.statement:
The frozen model assumptions do not identify the exact-dose causal curve.  More precisely, there exist compatible fixed constants, an observed law \(P\in\mathcal M\), and two admissible full-data extensions \(P^{\mathrm F}_1\) and \(P^{\mathrm F}_2\) satisfying every membership condition in \(\texttt{def:model-class}\), with the same \((W,A,Y)\)-marginal \(P\), such that, for every deterministic \(a\in[0,1]\),
\[
 \mathbb E_{P^{\mathrm F}_1}[Y(a)]=\theta(a)=a+\frac{1}{10},
 \qquad
 \mathbb E_{P^{\mathrm F}_2}[Y(a)]=a\ne\theta(a).
\]
Consequently the exact-dose causal mean is not identified, including on \(J\): consistency at the realized dose, sectionwise conditional exchangeability, strict overlap, smoothness of the observed regression, and continuity of a chosen conditional potential-outcome mean version do not force all admissible full-data extensions of an observed law to agree on \(\mathbb E[Y(a)]\).
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
We construct the two full-data extensions and verify every condition equation by equation.  Choose
\[
 d=1,\qquad s=7,\qquad \delta=\frac14,\qquad
 c_{\theta}=C_{\theta}=c_p=C_p=c_g=C_g=1,
 \qquad v_{\kappa}=V_{\kappa}=\frac1{100},\qquad B=2.
\]
The declared symbol ranges give \(d\in\mathbb N\), \(d>0\), \(s=7>3(d+1)=6\), and \(0<\delta<1/2\), hence \(J=[1/4,3/4]\).  The six one-condition compatibility requirements hold because
\[
 c_{\theta}=C_{\theta},\qquad c_p=1=C_p,\qquad
 c_g=1=C_g,\qquad v_{\kappa}=V_{\kappa}.
\]
These equalities verify \(\texttt{ass:theta-constant-compatibility}\), \(\texttt{ass:p-lower-compatibility}\), \(\texttt{ass:p-upper-compatibility}\), \(\texttt{ass:g-lower-compatibility}\), \(\texttt{ass:g-upper-compatibility}\), and \(\texttt{ass:variance-constant-compatibility}\).  Also,
\[
 \frac{c_{\theta}}2+\sqrt{v_{\kappa}}
 =\frac12+\frac1{10}=\frac35<2=B,
\]
which verifies \(\texttt{ass:bounded-witness-compatibility}\).

Consider the candidate observed-law primitives
\[
 p_\star(w)=1,\qquad g_\star(a\mid w)=1,\qquad
 m_\star(a,w)=a+\frac1{10},\qquad
 r_\star(a,w)=\left(a+\frac1{10}\right)^2+\frac1{100}.
\]
They are polynomials on compact cubes and therefore have finite \(C^7\) norms.  The quantity \(L_0\) in the frozen core is also finite because all functions entering its definition are polynomials.  Choose the fixed radius
\[
 L\ge \max\left\{L_0,\lVert p_\star\rVert_{C^7},
 \lVert g_\star\rVert_{C^7},\lVert m_\star\rVert_{C^7},
 \lVert r_\star\rVert_{C^7}\right\}.
\]
This choice verifies \(\texttt{ass:radius-compatibility}\), and it will verify each of the four radius-\(L\) smoothness conditions once the displayed functions are shown to be versions of the observed primitives.

On a probability space let \(W\), \(A\), and \(R\) be mutually independent, let \(W\) and \(A\) each be uniform on \([0,1]\), and impose
\[
 \Pr(R=1)=\Pr(R=-1)=\frac12.
\]
Define
\[
 Y=A+\frac1{10}R+\frac1{10},
\]
and let \(P\) be the law of \((W,A,Y)\).  Since \(0\le Y\le6/5<B\), \(\texttt{ass:outcome-bound}\) holds.  Mutual independence and uniformity provide the everywhere-defined density versions
\[
 p(w)=1,qquad g(a\mid w)=1,qquad
 f(a)=\int_0^1g(a\mid w)p(w)\,dw=1.
\]
Thus
\[
 \int_0^1p(w)\,dw=1,
 \qquad
 \int_0^1g(a\mid w)\,da=1\quad\text{for every }w\in[0,1],
\]
which verifies \(\texttt{ass:p-normalization}\) and \(\texttt{ass:g-normalization}\).  Because all four density-bound constants equal one, the same versions satisfy
\[
 c_p\le p(w)\le C_p,
 \qquad
 c_g\le g(a\mid w)\le C_g
\]
throughout their domains; this proves \(\texttt{ass:p-bounds}\) and \(\texttt{ass:overlap}\).  In particular, \(f(a)=1>0\), so every later division by \(f(a)\) is legitimate.

Direct conditioning, using \(\mathbb E[R]=0\) and \(R^2=1\), gives the everywhere-defined versions
\[
 m(a,w)=\mathbb E_P[Y\mid A=a,W=w]=a+\frac1{10}=m_\star(a,w)
\]
and
\[
 r(a,w)=\mathbb E_P[Y^2\mid A=a,W=w]
 =\left(a+\frac1{10}\right)^2+\frac1{100}=r_\star(a,w).
\]
Together with \(p=p_\star\), \(g=g_\star\), and the choice of \(L\), these identities verify \(\texttt{ass:p-smooth}\), \(\texttt{ass:g-smooth}\), \(\texttt{ass:m-smooth}\), and \(\texttt{ass:r-smooth}\).  By the definition of the observed-law functional \(\theta\) and the normalization of \(p\),
\[
 \theta(a)=\int_0^1m(a,w)p(w)\,dw=a+\frac1{10}
 \quad\text{for every }a\in[0,1].
\]
Hence \(\theta\) is nondecreasing, as required by \(\texttt{ass:monotone}\), and
\[
 \theta'(a)=1,
 \qquad c_{\theta}\le\theta'(a)\le C_{\theta}
 \quad\text{for every }a\in J,
\]
which verifies \(\texttt{ass:strict-slope}\).

The definitions of \(\sigma^2\) and \(e\) now yield
\[
 \sigma^2(a,w)=r(a,w)-m(a,w)^2=\frac1{100},
 \qquad e(a,w)=\frac{g(a\mid w)}{f(a)}=1.
\]
Using the definitions of \(\xi\) and \(\varepsilon\),
\[
 \varepsilon(O)=\frac{Y-m(A,W)}{e(A,W)}=\frac1{10}R.
\]
It follows that the constant conditional-moment version is
\[
 \kappa(a)=\mathbb E_P[\varepsilon(O)^2\mid A=a]
 =\frac1{100}=v_{\kappa}=V_{\kappa}
 \quad\text{for every }a\in J,
\]
which verifies \(\texttt{ass:variance}\) and its required positivity.

We next construct two full-data extensions of this same \(P\).  For every \(a\in[0,1]\), set
\[
 Y_1(a)=a+\frac1{10}R+\frac1{10},
 \qquad
 Y_2(a)=a+\frac1{10}R+\frac1{10}\mathbf 1\{a=A\}.
\]
The first map is Borel measurable in \((a,A,R)\).  The second is also Borel measurable because the diagonal \(\{(a,A):a=A\}\) is closed.  Consequently each sample path is Borel measurable and each coordinate evaluation is a random variable, so both processes are random elements of the evaluation-sigma-field space \(\mathcal Y_B\).  Moreover,
\[
 -\frac1{10}\le Y_j(a)\le\frac65<B
 \quad\text{for all }a\in[0,1]\text{ and }j\in\{1,2\},
\]
so the processes take values in the stipulated range \([-B,B]\).

For \(j\in\{1,2\}\), let \(P_j^{\mathrm F}\) be the law of
\[
 \bigl(W,A,Y,\{Y_j(a):a\in[0,1]\}\bigr).
\]
Its \((W,A,Y)\)-marginal is \(P\) by construction, proving \(\texttt{ass:observed-marginal}\).  Evaluation at the realized dose gives
\[
 Y_1(A)=A+\frac1{10}R+\frac1{10}=Y
\]
and
\[
 Y_2(A)=A+\frac1{10}R+\frac1{10}\mathbf 1\{A=A\}=Y.
\]
Thus each extension satisfies \(\texttt{ass:consistency}\).

Fix a deterministic \(a\in[0,1]\).  The continuous uniform law of \(A\) gives \(\Pr(A=a)=0\); hence
\[
 Y_1(a)=a+\frac1{10}R+\frac1{10}\quad\text{almost surely},
 \qquad
 Y_2(a)=a+\frac1{10}R\quad\text{almost surely}.
\]
Each right-hand side is a measurable function of \(R\), and \(R\) is independent of \((A,W)\).  Therefore, for bounded Borel functions \(h\) and \(q\),
\[
 \mathbb E\!\left[h\{Y_j(a)\}q(A)\mid W\right]
 =\mathbb E\!\left[h\{Y_j(a)\}\mid W\right]
  \mathbb E\!\left[q(A)\mid W\right]
 \quad\text{almost surely}.
\]
This conditional factorization proves \(Y_j(a)\perp A\mid W\) for each deterministic \(a\), and hence verifies \(\texttt{ass:exchangeability}\) for both extensions.

Since \(\mathbb E[R]=0\), define
\[
 \mu^{\mathrm F}_1(a,w)=a+\frac1{10},
 \qquad
 \mu^{\mathrm F}_2(a,w)=a.
\]
Both functions are jointly Borel measurable and continuous in \(a\) for every \(w\).  The preceding fixed-\(a\) almost-sure identities and the independence of \(R\) and \(W\) imply
\[
 \mu^{\mathrm F}_j(a,W)
 =\mathbb E_{P_j^{\mathrm F}}[Y_j(a)\mid W]
 \quad\text{almost surely for every fixed }a.
\]
Thus each is a version meeting every clause of \(\texttt{ass:potential-mean-continuity}\).

All observed-law membership conditions of \(\texttt{def:model-class}\) and all full-data extension conditions have now been verified.  Therefore \(P\in\mathcal M\), and \(P_1^{\mathrm F}\) and \(P_2^{\mathrm F}\) are two admissible witnesses for the same observed law.  Finally, for every deterministic \(a\in[0,1]\),
\[
 \mathbb E_{P_1^{\mathrm F}}[Y_1(a)]
 =a+\frac1{10}=\theta(a),
 \qquad
 \mathbb E_{P_2^{\mathrm F}}[Y_2(a)]
 =a\ne a+\frac1{10}=\theta(a).
\]
The modification in \(Y_2\) is supported on the random diagonal \(a=A\).  It is null in every deterministic-dose section, which preserves sectionwise exchangeability and the continuous conditional-mean versions, but consistency evaluates the process exactly on that diagonal.  The two admissible extensions therefore disagree at every deterministic dose, proving exact-dose nonidentification.

proposed_core_edits.reason: The negative identification certificate is a delivered root result, not a supporting lemma. The replacement proposition preserves and strengthens the explicit certificate to every deterministic dose. The immutable snapshot shows no inbound statement dependency on the obsolete lemma, so this promotion does not insert the proposition into any spatial-clock or other observed-law statistical result.

proposed_core_edits.proposed: The statistical target is the observed-law curve \(\theta(a)=\int m(a,w)p(w)\,dw\) for \(a\in J\). Proposition \(\texttt{prop:exact-dose-nonidentification}\) proves that the frozen model admits two admissible full-data extensions of the same observed law with different values of \(\mathbb E[Y(a)]\) at every deterministic dose. Thus \(\theta(a)\) is not identified with an exact-dose causal mean without an additional causal bridge.
proposed_core_edits.reason: The estimand line must cite the promoted root certificate and must distinguish the observed-law functional from the unidentifiable exact-dose causal mean.

prose_updates.tldr: Proposition \(\texttt{prop:exact-dose-nonidentification}\) proves, by two explicit random-diagonal full-data extensions of one observed law, that the frozen assumptions do not identify \(\mathbb E[Y(a)]\) at any deterministic dose. The paper therefore targets only the observed-law curve \(\theta(a)=\int m(a,w)p(w)\,dw\). On the likelihood-ratio side, the proved content is fixed-location finite-dimensional stationarity; exact Brownian scaling, which by itself gives no large-deviation principle or tail law; the proved deterministic action bracket \(1/2\le I_\star\le9/8\) with its single-plateau witness; the exact spatial-volume clock; centering algebra conditional on a future excursion expansion; and deterministic profile inversion. The contact-set analysis is an aspirational open-problem program, not a calibrated simultaneous causal band or a validated Gumbel procedure.

project_justification.gap: Proposition \(\texttt{prop:exact-dose-nonidentification}\) gives a constructive obstruction to causal interpretation: sectionwise exchangeability and a continuous conditional potential-outcome mean version permit random-diagonal changes that preserve the observed law and consistency while changing every deterministic-dose mean. Independently, Banerjee and Wellner (2001) provide only the fixed-location Brownian--GCM likelihood-ratio functional. Hooghiemstra and Lopuhaä (1998) rely on an explicit Markov argmax jump process, and Durot, Kulikov, and Lopuhaä (2012) transfer slope-error extremes through that process; neither result supplies an extreme-value theorem for the nonlocal likelihood-ratio energy.
project_justification.niche: The current contribution is a negative exact-dose identification certificate together with deterministic and fixed-location likelihood-ratio structure. A future research program could add a valid causal bridge and develop an infinite-domain GCM contact-set large-deviation principle, minimizer classification, sharp Palm expansion, anticlustering, marked-Poisson approximation, and a continuum-grid theorem. That program is aspirational and none of its probability conclusions is claimed here.
project_justification.fill: The completed results are Proposition \(\texttt{prop:exact-dose-nonidentification}\), fixed-location finite-dimensional stationarity, exact Brownian/GCM dilation, the proved deterministic bracket \(1/2\le I_\star\le9/8\), optimality of \(9/8\) within the full single-plateau family through minimization of \((1+r)^3/(6r)\) at \(r=1/2\), the explicit plateau witness, the exact observed-law spatial-volume clock, centering substitution conditional on a future affine-log excursion expansion, deterministic profile interval and image-set properties, and homogeneous reduction. No nuisance-rate theorem, optimized primitive-to-likelihood-ratio transfer theorem, tail rate, critical value, Poisson law, Gumbel law, simulation guarantee, or coverage theorem is retained.

sampling_model.design: The observed sample is iid from \(P\in\mathcal M\). Membership requires at least one full-data extension satisfying consistency, sectionwise conditional exchangeability, and conditional-potential-mean continuity, but Proposition \(\texttt{prop:exact-dose-nonidentification}\) proves that two admissible extensions of the same observed law may disagree on \(\mathbb E[Y(a)]\) for every deterministic dose.
sampling_model.nuisance_estimation: The cross-fitted primitive remains an observed-law construction, but no standalone learner-rate or optimized primitive-to-likelihood-ratio transfer theorem is retained. In particular, the present results do not establish a fitted-kernel maximal inequality, common contact localization, a slope envelope, or uniform stability of optimized likelihood-ratio values.

prose_updates.related_work: Banerjee and Wellner (2001) are used only for the finite fixed-location Brownian--GCM likelihood-ratio functional. Hooghiemstra and Lopuhaä (1998) derive extremes for a distinct Markov argmax process using its jump-transition machinery; Durot, Kulikov, and Lopuhaä (2012) transfer slope-error extremes through that argmax process, not likelihood-ratio-energy excursions. Doss (2026) supplies neighboring fixed-dose causal-isotonic likelihood-ratio work, while Takatsu and Westling (2025), Ai, Huang, and Zhang (2026), and Doss--VandenBerg supply neighboring simultaneous-band methods. None of those results is imported as a tail theorem for the nonlocal likelihood-ratio energy, and the present paper claims neither sharper bands, optimal width, tuning freedom, nor dominance over the Doss--VandenBerg multiscale Gaussian bands.
prose_updates.interpretation: The estimand \(\theta(a)=\int m(a,w)p(w)\,dw\) is an observed-law G-computation curve on \(J\), not an identified exact-dose causal curve: Proposition \(\texttt{prop:exact-dose-nonidentification}\) supplies two admissible extensions with different deterministic-dose means. For the AHA/CMS nurse-hours--readmission application, the current mathematics supports only an observed-law isotonic likelihood-ratio profile and the deterministic profile image set induced by an arbitrary common threshold. It does not support calibrated simultaneous causal reporting, a nominal confidence set for a threshold-crossing dose, or a Gumbel critical value.
prose_updates.technical_internal_limitation: Exact Brownian scaling gives \(\Pr\{D(0)>u\}=\Pr\{\Phi(u^{-1/2}\mathbb W)>1\}\), but no infinite-domain large-deviation principle or probability-tail conclusion follows from that identity. The proved deterministic action satisfies \(1/2\le I_\star\le9/8\), and the plateau value \(9/8\) is optimal only within the complete single-plateau family because \((1+r)^3/(6r)\) is minimized at \(r=1/2\). Missing probability ingredients are contact-set exponential tightness and continuity, global action-minimizer classification and uniqueness modulo translation, sharp Palm fluctuation and multiplicity analysis, conditional cluster-shape control, short-range anticlustering, marked-Poisson approximation, and a sample-path modulus/grid theorem. Separately, optimized observed-statistic transfer lacks the fitted-kernel maximal inequality, common localization, and slope-envelope arguments; no orphan nuisance-rate or transfer claim substitutes for those proofs.
prose_updates.honest_scope: Proposition \(\texttt{prop:exact-dose-nonidentification}\) proves that exact-dose causal identification fails under the frozen assumptions. The surviving positive results do not include a likelihood-ratio-energy tail rate, growing-domain coupling, critical value, feasible calibration, simulated-grid approximation, Poisson or Gumbel limit, or nominal simultaneous coverage theorem. The exact scaling identity carries no large-deviation or tail implication; the action bracket is deterministic; and the contact-set program is an aspirational open question not consumed by a proved theorem. The AHA/CMS output is therefore an observed-law profile and profile image set only. No claim is made about optimal width, tuning freedom, or dominance over the Doss--VandenBerg multiscale Gaussian bands.

statement_notes.justification: This root proposition is the paper's constructive negative certificate: two fully verified full-data extensions of one smooth, strictly increasing observed law disagree on every deterministic-dose causal mean.
statement_notes.gap: Sectionwise exchangeability and continuity of conditional potential-outcome mean versions do not constrain modifications supported on the random diagonal \(a=A\), although realized-dose consistency evaluates that diagonal.
statement_notes.consumer: The AHA/CMS nurse-hours--readmission analysis must describe \(\theta\) and its likelihood-ratio profile as observed-law objects until a separate causal bridge rules out the certified random-diagonal ambiguity.

proofs.proof_tex:
By \(\texttt{def:nonempty-witness}\), under \(P_0^{\mathrm F}\), \(W\) is uniform on \([0,1]^d\), \(A\) is uniform on \([0,1]\), and \(A\) is independent of \((W,R_0)\), where \(\mathbb P(R_0=1)=\mathbb P(R_0=-1)=1/2\). Moreover,
\[
Y(a)=c_{\theta}(a-1/2)+\sqrt{v_{\kappa}}R_0,
\qquad
Y=Y(A).
\]
Consequently the observed marginal \(P_0\) has the everywhere-defined density versions
\[
p(w)=1,
\qquad
g(a\mid w)=1.
\]
Since \(\mathbb E[R_0]=0\) and \(R_0^2=1\), independence gives, for every \((a,w)\in[0,1]^{d+1}\), the conditional-moment versions
\[
\begin{aligned}
m(a,w)
&=\mathbb E_{P_0}[Y\mid A=a,W=w]
=c_{\theta}(a-1/2)=m_0(a,w),\\
r(a,w)
&=\mathbb E_{P_0}[Y^2\mid A=a,W=w]
=m_0(a,w)^2+v_{\kappa}=r_0(a,w).
\end{aligned}
\]
The unit cube \([0,1]^d\) has Lebesgue volume one. Therefore the definitions of \(\theta\), \(\sigma^2\), \(f\), and \(\kappa\) yield
\[
\begin{aligned}
\theta(a)
&=\int_{[0,1]^d}m(a,w)p(w)\,dw
=c_{\theta}(a-1/2),\\
\theta'(a)&=c_{\theta},\\
\sigma^2(a,w)&=r(a,w)-m(a,w)^2=v_{\kappa},\\
f(a)&=\int_{[0,1]^d}g(a\mid w)p(w)\,dw=1,\\
\kappa(a)
&=f(a)\int_{[0,1]^d}\frac{\sigma^2(a,w)p(w)}{g(a\mid w)}\,dw
=v_{\kappa}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The division in the last line is valid because \(g(a\mid w)=1>0\).

We now verify every member condition of \(\texttt{def:model-class}\). The eight restrictions on the fixed constants follow, in their displayed order, from \(\texttt{ass:theta-constant-compatibility}\), \(\texttt{ass:p-lower-compatibility}\), \(\texttt{ass:p-upper-compatibility}\), \(\texttt{ass:g-lower-compatibility}\), \(\texttt{ass:g-upper-compatibility}\), \(\texttt{ass:variance-constant-compatibility}\), \(\texttt{ass:bounded-witness-compatibility}\), and \(\texttt{ass:radius-compatibility}\). The observed-coordinate marginal of \(P_0^{\mathrm F}\) is \(P_0\) by the construction, which verifies \(\texttt{ass:observed-marginal}\), and \(Y=Y(A)\) verifies \(\texttt{ass:consistency}\). For each deterministic \(a\), \(Y(a)\) is a measurable function of \(R_0\), whereas \(A\) is independent of \((W,R_0)\); hence \(Y(a)\perp A\mid W\), proving \(\texttt{ass:exchangeability}\). Also,
\[
\mathbb E_{P_0^{\mathrm F}}[Y(a)\mid W=w]
=c_{\theta}(a-1/2)=\mu^{\mathrm F}(a,w).
\]
This version is jointly measurable in \((a,w)\) and continuous in \(a\), so \(\texttt{ass:potential-mean-continuity}\) holds.

The triangle inequality, \(A\in[0,1]\), and \(\texttt{ass:bounded-witness-compatibility}\) give
\[
|Y|
\le c_{\theta}|A-1/2|+\sqrt{v_{\kappa}}
\le c_{\theta}/2+\sqrt{v_{\kappa}}
\le B,
\]
which proves \(\texttt{ass:outcome-bound}\). By the definition of \(L_0\), the functions \(p=1\), \(g=1\), \(m=m_0\), and \(r=r_0\) have the required \(C^s\) norms at most \(L_0\). Since \(L_0\le L\) by \(\texttt{ass:radius-compatibility}\), the four smoothness conditions \(\texttt{ass:p-smooth}\), \(\texttt{ass:g-smooth}\), \(\texttt{ass:m-smooth}\), and \(\texttt{ass:r-smooth}\) follow.

Because the dose interval and covariate cube both have Lebesgue volume one,
\[
\int_{[0,1]^d}p(w)\,dw=1,
\qquad
\int_0^1g(a\mid w)\,da=1
\quad\text{for every }w\in[0,1]^d.
\]
These equalities prove \(\texttt{ass:p-normalization}\) and \(\texttt{ass:g-normalization}\). Together with \(c_p\le1\le C_p\) and \(c_g\le1\le C_g\), they also verify \(\texttt{ass:p-bounds}\) and \(\texttt{ass:overlap}\). Finally, \(c_{\theta}>0\) and \(\theta'(a)=c_{\theta}\) make \(\theta\) nondecreasing on \([0,1]\). The compatibility inequalities \(c_{\theta}\le C_{\theta}\) and \(v_{\kappa}\le V_{\kappa}\) imply, for every \(a\in J\),
\[
c_{\theta}\le\theta'(a)=c_{\theta}\le C_{\theta},
\qquad
v_{\kappa}\le\kappa(a)=v_{\kappa}\le V_{\kappa}.
\]
Thus \(\texttt{ass:monotone}\), \(\texttt{ass:strict-slope}\), and \(\texttt{ass:variance}\) hold. Every defining condition of \(\mathcal M\) has been verified, so \(P_0\in\mathcal M\), with \(p=g=1\), \(\theta'=c_{\theta}\), and \(\kappa=v_{\kappa}\), as claimed.

Nonemptiness follows from \(\texttt{lem:model-nonempty}\), which supplies \(P_0\in\mathcal M\). Now fix \(P\in\mathcal M\). By \(\texttt{def:model-class}\) and \(\texttt{ass:monotone}\), its observed-law curve \(\theta\) is nondecreasing on \([0,1]\). The marginal density of \(A\) is
\[
f(a)=\int_{[0,1]^d}g(a\mid w)p(w)\,dw.
\]
The normalization \(\int_{[0,1]^d}p(w)\,dw=1\), the overlap bound \(g(a\mid w)\ge c_g\), and \(c_g>0\) imply, for every \(a\in[0,1]\),
\[
f(a)
\ge \int_{[0,1]^d}c_g p(w)\,dw
=c_g>0.
\]
In particular, the distribution function of \(A\) is
\[
P(A\le t)=\int_0^t f(a)\,da,
\qquad 0\le t\le1,
\]
and hence is absolutely continuous, and therefore continuous, with an everywhere positive density version. Thus both defining requirements of \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{WGC}}\) hold, proving
\[
\mathcal M\subseteq\mathcal M_{\mathrm{WGC}}.
\]

For strictness, construct an observed law \(Q\) as follows: \(W\) is uniform on \([0,1]^d\), \(A\) is uniform on \([0,1]\) and independent of \(W\), and \(Y=0\) almost surely. Under \(Q\), the versions
\[
p(w)=1,
\qquad
g(a\mid w)=1,
\qquad
m(a,w)=0
\]
give
\[
\theta(a)=\int_{[0,1]^d}m(a,w)p(w)\,dw=0.
\]
Therefore \(\theta\) is nondecreasing, while the marginal law of \(A\) is continuous with the everywhere positive density \(f=1\). It follows that \(Q\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{WGC}}\). On the other hand, \(\delta\in(0,1/2)\) implies \(1/2\in J=[\delta,1-\delta]\), whereas \(\theta'(1/2)=0<c_{\theta}\) because \(c_{\theta}>0\). Hence \(Q\) violates \(\texttt{ass:strict-slope}\), a member property in \(\texttt{def:model-class}\). This obstruction concerns the observed-law functional \(\theta\), so no choice of full-data extension can repair it. Thus \(Q\notin\mathcal M\), and consequently
\[
\varnothing\ne\mathcal M\subsetneq\mathcal M_{\mathrm{WGC}}.
\]

Finally, the descriptive membership assertion is a direct unpacking of \(\texttt{def:model-class}\): a member observed law admits at least one full-data extension satisfying the stated causal conditions and the jointly measurable continuous conditional-potential-mean version condition, while its observed marginal obeys the global radius-\(L\) \(C^s\) restrictions, the two-sided density restrictions, the strict-slope restriction on \(J\), and the two-sided effective-variance restriction on \(J\). This proves the entire proposition.

proofs.proof_tex:
Fix a finite deterministic collection \(x_1,\ldots,x_m\in\mathbb R\).  For \(x\in\mathbb R\), define the recentered increment path
\[
 \mathbb W_x(t)=\mathbb W(x+t)-\mathbb W(x),\qquad t\in\mathbb R.
\]
The definition of \(X\) in \(\texttt{def:canonical-field}\) gives the pathwise identity
\[
 X(x+t)-X(x)-2xt=\mathbb W_x(t)+t^2. \tag{1}
\]
We record the GCM equivariance used with (1).  If \(G\) is the greatest convex minorant of a function \(F\), then
\[
 \widetilde G(t)=G(x+t)-G(x)-2xt
\]
is the greatest convex minorant of
\(
 \widetilde F(t)=F(x+t)-F(x)-2xt
\).
Indeed, \(\widetilde G\) is convex and lies below \(\widetilde F\).  Conversely, translating and adding back the same affine function maps every convex minorant of \(\widetilde F\) to a convex minorant of \(F\), which must lie below \(G\).  The identical order argument on the two half-lines proves equivariance of the constrained one-sided minorants.  Under this transformation the slope constraint \(2x\) becomes the origin constraint \(0\), and both unrestricted and constrained slopes are reduced by \(2x\).  Changing variables in the energy integral of \(\texttt{def:canonical-field}\) therefore yields, on every path on which the fixed-location energies are defined,
\[
 D(x)=\Phi(\mathbb W_x). \tag{2}
\]

By the independent stationary Gaussian increment property of \(\mathbb W\) in \(\texttt{def:canonical-field}\), \(\mathbb W_x\) has the law of a two-sided standard Brownian motion.  Since \(D(0)=\Phi(\mathbb W)\), (2) implies
\[
 D(x)\stackrel{d}{=}D(0). \tag{3}
\]
The cited fixed-location result \(\texttt{lem:banerjee-wellner-fixed-location-lr}\) says that \(D(0)\) is a finite nonnegative random variable almost surely.  Equation (3) gives the same conclusion for each deterministic \(x_j\).  Because the collection is finite, intersecting the corresponding probability-one events proves simultaneous finiteness and nonnegativity of \(D(x_1),\ldots,D(x_m)\).

It remains to prove the joint, rather than merely marginal, stationarity assertion.  Fix \(r\in\mathbb R\).  For arbitrary indices \(i,j\) and times \(s,t\), the covariance
\[
 \operatorname{Cov}\!\left(\mathbb W_{x_i+r}(s),\mathbb W_{x_j+r}(t)\right)
\]
is the signed overlap of the two Brownian increment intervals with endpoints \((x_i+r,x_i+r+s)\) and \((x_j+r,x_j+r+t)\).  Translating all four endpoints by \(-r\) leaves that signed overlap unchanged.  Thus the centered Gaussian vector process
\[
 \bigl(\mathbb W_{x_1+r},\ldots,\mathbb W_{x_m+r}\bigr)
\]
has the same finite-dimensional distributions as
\(
 \bigl(\mathbb W_{x_1},\ldots,\mathbb W_{x_m}\bigr)
\).
Applying the measurable fixed-location functional \(\Phi\) coordinatewise in (2) gives
\[
 (D(x_1+r),\ldots,D(x_m+r))
 \stackrel{d}{=}(D(x_1),\ldots,D(x_m)). \tag{4}
\]
Only finitely many fixed-location functionals enter this argument.  Consequently, (1)--(4) prove no separability, local boundedness, continuum contact-radius control, or block independence, in agreement with the stated scope.

For a deterministic perturbation \(h\), put \(F_h(t)=t^2+h(t)\).  If \(h_b(t)=b^2h(t/b)\) for \(b>0\), then
\[
 F_{h_b}(t)=b^2F_h(t/b). \tag{1}
\]
Let \(G_h\) be the unrestricted greatest convex minorant of \(F_h\).  The function \(t\mapsto b^2G_h(t/b)\) is convex and lies below the right-hand side of (1).  Conversely, applying the inverse dilation to any convex minorant of \(F_{h_b}\) produces a convex minorant of \(F_h\).  Maximality on both sides therefore gives
\[
 G_{h_b}(t)=b^2G_h(t/b). \tag{2}
\]
The same order-preserving argument on the left and right half-lines gives (2) for the origin-constrained minorants.  Hence every corresponding slope is multiplied by \(b\).  With the substitution \(t=bs\), the defining difference of squared-slope energies in \(\texttt{def:excursion-regime}\) becomes
\[
 \Phi(h_b)=b^3\Phi(h), \tag{3}
\]
whenever the two energies are defined.

If \(h\) is absolutely continuous, then \(h_b'(t)=b h'(t/b)\) for almost every \(t\).  The condition \(h'\in L^2(\mathbb R)\) and a change of variables give
\[
 \frac12\lVert h_b'\rVert_2^2
 =\frac12\int_{\mathbb R}b^2\{h'(t/b)\}^2\,dt
 =b^3\frac12\lVert h'\rVert_2^2. \tag{4}
\]

Fix \(u>0\), set \(b=u^{1/3}\), and set \(\epsilon=u^{-1/2}=b^{-3/2}\).  Brownian self-similarity, which follows by comparing the zero means and covariances of the two centered Gaussian processes, gives
\[
 b^{1/2}\mathbb W(\,\cdot\,/b)\stackrel{d}{=}\mathbb W.
\]
Moreover,
\[
 (\epsilon\mathbb W)_b(t)
 =b^2\epsilon\mathbb W(t/b)
 =b^{1/2}\mathbb W(t/b).
\]
Using the fixed-location well-posedness from \(\texttt{lem:canonical-wellposedness}\), the identity \(D(0)=\Phi(\mathbb W)\) from \(\texttt{def:canonical-field}\), and (3), we obtain
\[
 D(0)\stackrel{d}{=}\Phi((\epsilon\mathbb W)_b)
 =b^3\Phi(\epsilon\mathbb W)
 =u\Phi(u^{-1/2}\mathbb W).
\]
Therefore
\[
 \Pr\{D(0)>u\}=\Pr\{\Phi(u^{-1/2}\mathbb W)>1\}. \tag{5}
\]

We next establish the lower action bound without interpreting it as a probability-tail rate.  Let \(h(0)=0\), let \(h'\in L^2(\mathbb R)\), and write
\[
 y(t)=2t+h'(t).
\]
On a finite interval, let \(g\) denote the unrestricted GCM slope of a primitive of \(y\).  If \(G\) is that GCM and \(H=F_h-G\), then \(H\ge0\), the positive measure \(dg\) is carried by the contact set \(\{H=0\}\), and \(H\) vanishes at the relevant endpoints.  For every nondecreasing slope competitor \(v\), integration by parts gives
\[
 \int (y-g)(v-g)
 =-\int H\,dv+\int H\,dg
 \le0. \tag{6}
\]
On the two half-intervals the same calculation applies to the constrained slope \(g^0\); the possible boundary term at the split has nonpositive sign because the left slope is capped at zero and the right slope is floored at zero.  Thus (6) is also the variational inequality for the origin-constrained cone.  Both slope classes are convex cones.  Taking successively the competitors \(0\) and \(2g\), and then \(0\) and \(2g^0\), in their respective inequalities yields
\[
 \int (y-g)g=0,
 \qquad
 \int (y-g^0)g^0=0. \tag{7}
\]
Expanding squares and using (7) shows that the constrained-versus-unconstrained residual sum-of-squares difference equals the likelihood-ratio energy:
\[
 \int\{(y-g^0)^2-(y-g)^2\}
 =\int\{g^2-(g^0)^2\}. \tag{8}
\]
The linear slope \(\ell(t)=2t\) is nondecreasing and satisfies the origin split constraint.  Hence least-squares optimality of \(g^0\), nonnegativity of squared loss, and (8) imply on every finite interval
\[
 0\le \Phi(h)
 \le \int\{y(t)-\ell(t)\}^2\,dt
 =\int\{h'(t)\}^2\,dt. \tag{9}
\]
For an infinite-domain energy, apply the preceding argument on an increasing sequence of finite contact intervals.  The defining GCM energies are the corresponding exhaustion limits whenever \(\Phi(h)\) is well defined, while the right side increases to \(\lVert h'\rVert_2^2\).  Thus (9) remains valid on \(\mathbb R\).  In particular, \(\Phi(h)\ge1\) implies
\[
 \frac12\lVert h'\rVert_2^2\ge\frac12.
\]
Taking the infimum in \(\texttt{def:excursion-regime}\) proves
\[
 I_\star\ge\frac12. \tag{10}
\]

For the upper bound, let \(k=4^{1/3}\), let \(a=k/4\), and define the absolutely continuous perturbation by \(h(0)=0\) and
\[
 h'(t)=(k-2t)\mathbf 1\{-a\le t\le k/2\}. \tag{11}
\]
This derivative has compact support and is square integrable.  The derivative of \(F_h\) is
\[
 y(t)=2t+h'(t)=
 \begin{cases}
 2t,&t<-a,\\
 k,&-a\le t\le k/2,\\
 2t,&t>k/2.
 \end{cases} \tag{12}
\]
Since \(-2a=-k/2<k\) and \(2(k/2)=k\), the function in (12) is nondecreasing.  Thus \(F_h\) is convex and its unrestricted GCM slope is \(y\).  By the cap-and-floor construction in \(\texttt{def:canonical-field}\), the origin-constrained slope is
\[
 g^0(t)=
 \begin{cases}
 0,&-a\le t\le0,\\
 y(t),&t\notin[-a,0].
 \end{cases} \tag{13}
\]
Indeed, to the left of the origin the only portion of the unrestricted slope exceeding zero is the plateau in (12), and to the right it is already bounded below by zero.  Equations (12)--(13) therefore give
\[
 \Phi(h)=\int_{-a}^{0}k^2\,dt=ak^2=\frac{k^3}{4}=1. \tag{14}
\]
The action of this perturbation is
\[
 \frac12\lVert h'\rVert_2^2
 =\frac12\int_{-a}^{k/2}(k-2t)^2\,dt
 =\frac{(k+2a)^3}{12}
 =\frac{(3k/2)^3}{12}
 =\frac98. \tag{15}
\]
Thus the witness is admissible for the action problem and proves \(I_\star\le9/8\).

For clarity about maximality, the same calculation for the full one-plateau family with arbitrary \(k,a>0\) gives \(\Phi(h)=ak^2\).  Under the unit-energy restriction \(ak^2=1\), put \(r=2a/k>0\).  Then \(k^3=2/r\), and the action is
\[
 \frac{(k+2a)^3}{12}=\frac{(1+r)^3}{6r}. \tag{16}
\]
Its derivative has the sign of \(2r-1\), so (16) is minimized at \(r=1/2\), where it equals \(9/8\).  Hence (11) is optimal within this one-plateau family, but (10) and (15) give only the global bracket
\[
 \frac12\le I_\star\le\frac98.
\]
Neither the bracket, the within-family optimization, nor the exact scaling identity supplies an infinite-domain large-deviation principle, a sharp tail rate, a Palm intensity, or an extreme-value limit.

Fix \(P\in\mathcal M\) and \(a\in J\).  By \(\texttt{ass:p-normalization}\), \(\int p(w)\,dw=1\), and by \(\texttt{ass:overlap}\),
\(
 c_g\le g(a\mid w)\le C_g
\)
for every \(w\).  Since \(p\ge0\), the definition of \(f\) gives
\[
 c_g=c_g\int p(w)\,dw
 \le f(a)=\int g(a\mid w)p(w)\,dw
 \le C_g\int p(w)\,dw=C_g. \tag{1}
\]
The assumptions \(\texttt{ass:strict-slope}\) and \(\texttt{ass:variance}\) give
\[
 0<c_\theta\le\theta'(a)\le C_\theta,
 \qquad
 0<v_\kappa\le\kappa(a)\le V_\kappa. \tag{2}
\]
Thus every factor divided by in the definition of \(h_n(a)\) is strictly positive.  Combining (1)--(2), with division only by positive quantities, yields
\[
 \left(\frac{4v_\kappa}{nC_gC_\theta^2}\right)^{1/3}
 \le h_n(a)\le
 \left(\frac{4V_\kappa}{nc_gc_\theta^2}\right)^{1/3}. \tag{3}
\]
Multiplication by \(n^{1/3}>0\) proves the first displayed bound in the theorem.

Inverting the positive defining expression gives
\[
 h_n(a)^{-1}=n^{1/3}
 \left\{\frac{f(a)\theta'(a)^2}{4\kappa(a)}\right\}^{1/3}. \tag{4}
\]
Taking reciprocals in (3) places the right side of (4) between
\[
 n^{1/3}\left(\frac{c_gc_\theta^2}{4V_\kappa}\right)^{1/3}
 \quad\hbox{and}\quad
 n^{1/3}\left(\frac{C_gC_\theta^2}{4v_\kappa}\right)^{1/3}. \tag{5}
\]
For \(a_1<a_2\) in \(J\), integrating (5) gives
\[
 n^{1/3}\left(\frac{c_gc_\theta^2}{4V_\kappa}\right)^{1/3}(a_2-a_1)
 \le \Psi_{n,P}(a_2)-\Psi_{n,P}(a_1)
 \le n^{1/3}\left(\frac{C_gC_\theta^2}{4v_\kappa}\right)^{1/3}(a_2-a_1). \tag{6}
\]
Both constants are finite and strictly positive, so \(\Psi_{n,P}\) is strictly increasing and bi-Lipschitz.  Since \(\Psi_{n,P}(\inf J)=0\), its image is an interval whose length is \(\Psi_{n,P}(\sup J)\).  Integrating (4) and using \(\texttt{def:spatial-clock}\) proves the exact identity
\[
 \Psi_{n,P}(\sup J)
 =n^{1/3}\int_J
 \left\{\frac{f(a)\theta'(a)^2}{4\kappa(a)}\right\}^{1/3}\,da
 =n^{1/3}\mathcal V(P)=T_n(P). \tag{7}
\]
All constants in (3), (5), and (6) depend only on the fixed model constants.  The bounds are therefore uniform over \(P\in\mathcal M\) and \(a\in J\).  The proof is entirely observed-law algebra and makes no coupling or stochastic-transfer assertion.

Assume that \(f(a)=f_0\), \(\theta'(a)=r_0\), and \(\kappa(a)=\kappa_0\) on \(J\), where the three constants are positive.  Direct substitution into \(\texttt{def:spatial-clock}\) gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \mathcal V(P)
 &=\int_J\left(\frac{f_0r_0^2}{4\kappa_0}\right)^{1/3}\,da
 =|J|\left(\frac{f_0r_0^2}{4\kappa_0}\right)^{1/3},\\
 T_n(P)
 &=n^{1/3}\mathcal V(P)
 =n^{1/3}|J|\left(\frac{f_0r_0^2}{4\kappa_0}\right)^{1/3}.
 \end{aligned} \tag{1}
\]
The inverse local scale from \(\texttt{thm:causal-transfer}\) is constant in \(a\):
\[
 h_n(a)^{-1}=n^{1/3}
 \left(\frac{f_0r_0^2}{4\kappa_0}\right)^{1/3}. \tag{2}
\]
Integrating (2) from \(\inf J\) to \(a\) shows that \(\Psi_{n,P}\) is affine, and evaluating it at \(\sup J\) gives exactly the image length in (1).

For the fixed-location assertion, apply \(\texttt{lem:canonical-wellposedness}\) with \(m=1\), \(x_1=0\), and common shift \(r=x\).  Its finite-dimensional stationarity conclusion gives
\[
 D(x)\stackrel{d}{=}D(0). \tag{3}
\]
The proof of that lemma obtains (3) by translating the constraint and subtracting the affine tangent, which is precisely translation and affine GCM equivariance.  Equations (1)--(3) are constant-coefficient and fixed-location identities only; they imply neither a growing-domain excursion theorem nor statistical calibration.

added_lemmas.statement: For the fixed origin constraint, the Brownian--GCM likelihood-ratio functional \(D(0)\) in \(\texttt{def:canonical-field}\) is a finite nonnegative random variable almost surely.

proofs.proof_tex:
Fix a realized sample and a point \(a\in J\).  Put \(k=k(a)\), \(z_i=Z_{(i)}\), and define
\[
 F(v)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(z_i-v_i)^2,
 \qquad
 H_k(t)=\{v\in\mathcal C_n:v_k=t\},
 \qquad
 L_k(t)=\min_{v\in H_k(t)}F(v).
\]
For each \(t\in\mathbb R\), the constant vector \(t\mathbf 1\) belongs to \(H_k(t)\), so this feasible set is nonempty.  By the definition
\[
 \mathcal C_n=\{v\in\mathbb R^n:v_1\le\cdots\le v_n\},
\]
the cone \(\mathcal C_n\) is closed and convex.  Hence \(H_k(t)\), being its intersection with the closed affine hyperplane \(\{v:v_k=t\}\), is closed and convex.  The objective \(F(v)=\lVert v-z\rVert_2^2\) is continuous and coercive on \(\mathbb R^n\).  Consequently, its minimum over the nonempty closed set \(H_k(t)\) is attained and finite.  The same argument applies to the nonempty closed cone \(\mathcal C_n\), and therefore
\[
 c_0:=\min_{v\in\mathcal C_n}F(v)=F(\widehat u)
\]
is finite and attained.  From \(H_k(t)\subseteq\mathcal C_n\) and \(\texttt{def:lr-profile}\),
\[
 Q_n(a,t)=L_k(t)-c_0\ge 0. \tag{1}
\]

We next show that \(t\mapsto Q_n(a,t)\) is convex.  Let \(t_1,t_2\in\mathbb R\), let \(v^{(j)}\in H_k(t_j)\) attain \(L_k(t_j)\), and fix \(\lambda\in[0,1]\).  Convexity of \(\mathcal C_n\) and linearity of the coordinate map give
\[
 \lambda v^{(1)}+(1-\lambda)v^{(2)}
 \in H_k\bigl(\lambda t_1+(1-\lambda)t_2\bigr).
\]
Since a squared Euclidean norm is convex,
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 L_k\bigl(\lambda t_1+(1-\lambda)t_2\bigr)
 &\le F\bigl(\lambda v^{(1)}+(1-\lambda)v^{(2)}\bigr)\\
 &\le \lambda F(v^{(1)})+(1-\lambda)F(v^{(2)})\\
 &=\lambda L_k(t_1)+(1-\lambda)L_k(t_2).
 \end{aligned} \tag{2}
\]
Subtracting the constant \(c_0\) proves the asserted convexity of \(Q_n(a,\cdot)\).

Now realize the extended-nonnegative threshold \(\widehat q_{n,\alpha}\).  If \(\widehat q_{n,\alpha}<\infty\), then the stipulated range \(\widehat\kappa(a)\in(0,\infty)\) implies
\[
 c(a):=\widehat\kappa(a)\widehat q_{n,\alpha}\in[0,\infty).
\]
By (2), the sublevel set
\[
 \{t\in\mathbb R:Q_n(a,t)\le c(a)\}
\]
is convex and hence is an interval in \(\mathbb R\).  It is nonempty: if \(t=\widehat u_k\), then \(\widehat u\in H_k(t)\), whence
\[
 c_0\le L_k(\widehat u_k)\le F(\widehat u)=c_0,
 \qquad
 Q_n(a,\widehat u_k)=0\le c(a). \tag{3}
\]
If instead \(\widehat q_{n,\alpha}=+\infty\), finiteness of \(L_k(t)\) and \(c_0\) implies \(Q_n(a,t)<\infty\) for every \(t\), so the sublevel set is all of \(\mathbb R\).  By \(\texttt{def:profile-band}\), this proves the claimed interval structure of \(\mathcal C_n(a)\), including the allowed value \(\mathbb R\).

Define the realized common profile event
\[
 E:=\{\theta(a)\in\mathcal C_n(a)\text{ for every }a\in J\}.
\]
For every \(a\in J\), positivity of \(\widehat\kappa(a)\) and \(\texttt{def:profile-band}\) give
\[
 \theta(a)\in\mathcal C_n(a)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \frac{Q_n(a,\theta(a))}{\widehat\kappa(a)}
 \le \widehat q_{n,\alpha}. \tag{4}
\]
Taking the conjunction of (4) over the nonempty interval \(J=[\delta,1-\delta]\), and using the definition of a supremum together with \(\texttt{def:lr-profile}\), yields
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 E
 &=\left\{\frac{Q_n(a,\theta(a))}{\widehat\kappa(a)}
       \le\widehat q_{n,\alpha}\text{ for every }a\in J\right\}\\
 &=\left\{\sup_{a\in J}
       \frac{Q_n(a,\theta(a))}{\widehat\kappa(a)}
       \le\widehat q_{n,\alpha}\right\}\\
 &=\{S_n(\theta)\le\widehat q_{n,\alpha}\}. \tag{5}
 \end{aligned}
\]
When \(\widehat q_{n,\alpha}=+\infty\), both sides of (5) are the whole realized sample space, so the same equality remains valid.

Finally, on \(E\), the restriction of \(\theta\) to \(J\) selects an element of \(\mathcal C_n(a)\) at every \(a\in J\).  Assumption \(\texttt{ass:monotone}\) says that \(\theta\) is nondecreasing on \([0,1]\), hence also on \(J\).  Thus \(\theta\) is one of the curves mapped in \(\texttt{def:crossing-set}\), and the image of this selector is
\[
 \inf\{a\in J:\theta(a)\ge\zeta\}=\tau_\zeta, \tag{6}
\]
with the same empty-set and left-endpoint conventions on both sides.  Equation (6) proves that the profile image set contains \(\tau_\zeta\) on \(E\).  The argument is deterministic conditional on the realized sample.  In particular, (5) transfers whatever probability a separately chosen threshold gives to the common event, but neither the definitions nor this proposition assign that event a nominal probability.
